report.title: EU AI Act Obligations for General-Purpose AI (GPAI) Model Providers in 2026
report.body_markdown:
## Executive Summary

Under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act framework, obligations for providers of General-Purpose AI (GPAI) models operate alongside transparency and risk-management requirements across phased milestones [1], [2]. Official European Commission institutional records establish that primary AI Act obligations specifically applicable to providers of GPAI models entered into application on 2 August 2025 [1]. Consequently, by 2026, baseline GPAI provider requirements are already active and enforceable [1], [3].

In 2026, additional transparency rules take effect, including obligations under Article 50 applicable from 2 August 2026 concerning the marking, labelling, and transparency of AI-generated and generative content [1], [4], [5]. These rules complement the existing GPAI model obligations [4]. Enforcement and compliance mechanisms in 2026 involve the European AI Office, national market surveillance authorities, the GPAI Code of Practice, and dedicated complaints and whistleblower tools [2], [3], [6].

## Analysis

### Status of GPAI Model Obligations in 2026

According to official European Commission milestones, the core AI Act obligations directed at providers of GPAI models took effect on 2 August 2025 following the publication of Commission guidelines and the GPAI Code of Practice in July 2025 [1], [3]. Therefore, throughout 2026, GPAI model providers must maintain compliance with:

- The applicable rules for general-purpose AI models, supported by the European Commission's Guidelines for providers of GPAI models and the GPAI Code of Practice [1], [3].
- Operational compliance supervision administered under the European AI Office and Commission enforcement mechanisms, including whistleblower and downstream provider complaints channels [3].

### Requirements Taking Effect or Expanding in 2026

In 2026, regulatory focus broadens to include general and generative AI transparency rules:

- **Transparency Obligations (Article 50):** Applicable from 2 August 2026, transparency obligations for providers and deployers of generative AI systems address risks of deception and manipulation to protect the integrity of the information ecosystem [4], [5]. These requirements explicitly complement the GPAI model rules [4].
- **Code of Practice and Guidelines:** Commission milestones record the publication of the Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content (June 2026) and guidelines on transparency obligations (July 2026) [1], [7].

### Enforcement and Penalties

Enforcement for non-compliance with applicable AI Act provisions is carried out by National Market Surveillance Authorities, the European AI Office (for systems under its direct supervision), and the European Data Protection Supervisor (for EU institutions) [6]. Fines for breaches can reach up to €15 million or 3% of global annual turnover for companies, with proportionality considerations applied to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and small mid-cap companies (SMCs) [6].

## Timeline and Applicability

Official EU institutional sources document the regulatory rollout timeline as follows:

- **1 August 2024:** Entry into force of the EU AI Act [6].
- **10–18 July 2025:** Commission receives the GPAI Code of Practice and publishes guidelines for GPAI providers [1].
- **2 August 2025:** AI Act obligations for providers of GPAI models enter into application [1].
- **June–July 2026:** Publication of the Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content and guidelines on transparency obligations [1], [7].
- **2 August 2026:** Transparency obligations under Article 50 for providers and deployers of generative AI systems enter into full application [1], [4], [5].

## Limitations and Uncertainty

This analysis relies exclusively on primary European Commission documentation and institutional portal publications. Detailed sub-article operational standards not quoted directly in the verified source snapshots are bounded by available official institutional guidance.
